title: Antinous and the Nile
author: Historia Augusta

edition.name: Historia Augusta, Latin text of the Loeb Classical Library edition (D. Magie), as presented on LacusCurtius (Bill Thayer), whose Latin pages credit "a Loeb Classical Library" edition of MCMXXI (1921); public domain

source_text: Antinoum suum, dum per Nilum navigat, perdidit, quem muliebriter flevit. de quo varia fama est, aliis eum devotum pro Hadriano adserentibus, aliis quod et forma eius ostentat et nimia voluptas Hadriani. et Graeci quidem volente Hadriano eum consecraverunt, oracula per eum dari adserentes, quae Hadrianus ipse composuisse iactatur.
excerpt_note: Sections 14.5–7 complete. The edition begins sections 6 and 7 in lower case after a full stop, and so does this text.

translation: He lost his Antinous while sailing along the Nile, and wept for him like a woman. About him the reports vary: some claim that he had offered himself to death for Hadrian, others claim what both his beauty and Hadrian's excessive sensuality suggest. The Greeks, at Hadrian's wish, did indeed make him a god, claiming that oracles were given through him, oracles that Hadrian himself is rumoured to have composed.
translation_note: The second sentence is compressed: aliīs (adserentibus) quod ... ostentat, "others (claiming) what ... suggests"; the writer leaves the sexual implication unspoken. Hadriānus ... composuisse iactātur is a personal passive: "Hadrian is said to have composed".

essay.t: Antinous came from Bithynium, also called Claudiopolis, in Bithynia, and Cassius Dio calls him a favourite of the emperor Hadrian and speaks of Hadrian's love for him.
He died in the waters of the Nile in AD 130.
Our passage gives the bare event and then the gossip.
Hadrian, it says, wept for him "like a woman", a phrase that judges the emperor's open grief by Roman ideas of how a man should behave.
It then reports two explanations: some said Antinous had offered his life for Hadrian, others pointed to what his beauty and Hadrian's excessive sensuality suggested.
The second explanation hints at a sexual relationship without stating it; the text is insinuating rather than informative.
Cassius Dio gives the same alternatives more sharply.

Hadrian himself wrote that Antinous died by falling into the Nile, but Dio says "the truth" is that he was offered in sacrifice, perhaps having volunteered to die so that a life could be given for Hadrian's purposes.

Neither account can be checked: Dio's book survives only in an abridgement, and the Historia Augusta was written by a single author near the end of the fourth century, under six false names, and its checkable claims have often proved unfounded.
An accident remains as possible as any of the darker stories.
According to our passage, the Greeks made Antinous a god at Hadrian's wish and claimed he gave oracles, which Hadrian himself was rumoured to have written.
Dio adds that Hadrian founded a city where Antinous died and named it after him, set up statues of him almost everywhere, and claimed to have seen his star, which people mocked.

The city was Antinoopolis, and a statue of Antinous as the Egyptian god Osiris, found in 1740 at Hadrian's Villa near Tivoli, is now in the Vatican Museums; the museum says his cult spread rapidly between 133 and 138.
